Amends: [2026-11-13-shared-record-behind-a-store-port.md](2026-11-13-shared-record-behind-a-store-port.md), the record-size limit. Every store refuses a record past `recordLimit`, and a refused record never lists; a batch may still land in part, as the port allows.

## Problem

Every record store refuses a record past core's `recordLimit`, 4 MiB. A head that changes many workspace manifests makes one guardrails finding per manifest, each naming the scripts it changes, and their record can pass the limit. The store then refused the round's records after the harness had stored a verdict of findings, so the review threw a store error with that verdict standing.

Example: 1,500 changed manifests, each naming twenty long scripts, wrote a guardrails record of about 5 MB.

## Choice

- Past the limit, the guardrails check leaves out the detail of its last findings in ID order, as `SightingBudget.checkRecord.fit` does. A trimmed finding keeps its ID, rule, severity, resolution, place and What to do, so what blocks is unchanged. Its Why here names how many files lost their detail and says that `git diff` shows them. A finding that trimming would not make smaller keeps its detail.

message.text: The new decision declares that it amends only the store-port decision. But its Choice changes what a guardrails notice says, and the active base decision "Every npm script the base had counts as a switch-off" (2026-11-20) governs exactly that. That decision exists because a notice on a changed `package.json` "said only which analyser the file configures" and "gave no sign that the gate's own command changed". Its fix puts each switch-off sentence ("It changes the npm script \"check\"", "It turns Biome's linter off", "It turns on noCheck") in the notice's What, guardrails.ts:343-355. It keeps the notice under the 4 MiB record by quoting at most ten names, base line 22. `Finding.abridged` replaces What with the headline "Review the change to <path>, which configures <analyser>.". It replaces Why here, "…a switched-off check reads as a clean one", with the trim note. So every abridged notice reads exactly like the notice that base decision retired.

## Problem

The store then refused the round's records after the harness had stored a verdict of findings, so the review threw a store error with that verdict standing.

Example: 1,500 changed manifests, each naming twenty long scripts, wrote a guardrails record of about 5 MB.

## Choice

- Past the limit, the guardrails check leaves out the detail of its last findings in ID order, as `SightingBudget.checkRecord.fit` does. A trimmed finding keeps its ID, rule, severity, resolution, place and What to do, so what blocks is unchanged. Its Why here names how many files lost their detail and says that `git diff` shows them. A finding that trimming would not make smaller keeps its detail.

CI runs `npm run check` from the head's own `package.json`. So a head that rewrites that script makes the gate do less, or nothing, and CI still reads green. Melian's notice on a changed `package.json` said only which analyser the file configures. It named a switch-off only when the head deleted the file.

Example: a head changes `"check": "biome check … && vitest --run"` to `"check": "true"`. Every CI job passes, and the notice gave no sign that the gate's own command changed.

## Rule

`switchOffs` in `packages/core/src/analyser.ts` names each script the base's `package.json` had that the head changes or removes. It reads any `package.json` in any letter case of the name, but guardrails passes it only the manifests its notice already covers: the root's and each workspace package's. A script whose value differs as JSON is changed. A script missing from the head's `scripts`, or every script when the head's `scripts` is absent or not an object, is removed. A script the head only adds, and a change to any other field, add nothing. It reads both revisions as npm's `json-parse-even-better-errors` does: it strips one leading byte order mark, then calls `JSON.parse`. It does not use the JSON-with-comments reader of the tsconfig and Biome checks. That reader drops a comma before `}` or `]` even inside a string, so `"echo ,}"` and `"echo }"` read as the same script. When the base had scripts and the head's file does not read as a JSON object, the notice says Melian cannot read the head's scripts. That covers a malformed file, a file too large to read, and a symbolic link, whose blob is its target's path though npm follows it to a file whose scripts run.

The notice quotes only script names, as JSON strings, and takes them from the base. No text from the head reaches the stored finding: a head's script value, or a name the head adds, never appears in it. JSON quoting keeps a newline or quote in a base name from reading as prose. Each sentence quotes at most ten names of at most 100 characters and counts the rest, since one guardrails record holds every changed manifest's notice and the record store takes at most 4 MiB.

This changes the notice's words, not what blocks. The notice on a changed `package.json` already blocks at `analyserSeverity`.

But its Choice changes what a guardrails notice says, and the active base decision "Every npm script the base had counts as a switch-off" (2026-11-20) governs exactly that. That decision exists because a notice on a changed `package.json` "said only which analyser the file configures" and "gave no sign that the gate's own command changed". Its fix puts each switch-off sentence ("It changes the npm script \"check\"", "It turns Biome's linter off", "It turns on noCheck") in the notice's What, guardrails.ts:343-355. It keeps the notice under the 4 MiB record by quoting at most ten names, base line 22. `Finding.abridged` replaces What with the headline "Review the change to <path>, which configures <analyser>.". explanation.whatToDo: Either declare `Amends:` on the every-npm-script decision and get a ruling that the switch-off sentences may be dropped, or keep them when abridging. For example, keep the `switchOffs` sentences (already capped at ten names) in the abridged What and drop only the remaining detail, or exempt notices that carry a switch-off from the trim and fail closed when the rest cannot fit.
explanation.whyHere: The head decision sets its own standard ("what blocks is unchanged") and says nothing about the switch-off wording, the one thing the base decision guards. The base decision itself says the change is to the notice's words, not to what blocks. So keeping the blocking set does not keep that decision's reason. `runCheck` trims every guardrails finding together in ID order, the root manifest's notice included. Whether the gate's own command is named now depends on where that notice's ID sorts and on how many other manifests the head touches.

properties.failureScenario: A head runs a codemod across 1,500 workspace manifests, each changing twenty long script names (the change's own CLI test fixture), and also changes the root `package.json` from `"check": "biome check … && vitest --run"` to `"check": "true"`. evaluateGuardrails writes 1,501 notices. Their record passes `SightingBudget.checkRecord`, so `runCheck` (checks.ts:327) calls `fit`. `fit` sorts by ID and abridges every notice after the latest cut that fits. In the CLI test that is a large share of the 1,500. When the root notice's ID sorts after the cut, `abridged` (findings.ts:1949-1955) sets its What to "Review the change to package.json, which configures Biome and tsc." and its Why here to "Melian left out the detail for N more files…". The sentence "It changes the npm script \"check\"" is gone from the local finding, the shared record and the published comment. The maintainer asked to acknowledge the notice gets no sign that CI's gate command became `true`, which is the base decision's exact problem example. A head author can also add manifests until the cut moves before the root notice.

trigger.snippet:
# A guardrails record fits the store, or its check fails

Status: the maintainer ruled, on [issue #605](https://github.com/melian-agent/melian/issues/605), that a guardrails record must fit the store's 4 MiB record limit, and that one which cannot fit even with every finding's detail left out fails closed. Trimming the check's own findings, rather than only the exported record, is the builder's choice, which the coordinator agreed on 2026-11-20; it is not a ruling.

Amends: [2026-11-13-shared-record-behind-a-store-port.md](2026-11-13-shared-record-behind-a-store-port.md), the record-size limit. Every store refuses a record past `recordLimit`, and a refused record never lists; a batch may still land in part, as the port allows.

## Problem

Every record store refuses a record past core's `recordLimit`, 4 MiB. A head that changes many workspace manifests makes one guardrails finding per manifest, each naming the scripts it changes, and their record can pass the limit. The store then refused the round's records after the harness had stored a verdict of findings, so the review threw a store error with that verdict standing.

Example: 1,500 changed manifests, each naming twenty long scripts, wrote a guardrails record of about 5 MB.

## Choice

- Past the limit, the guardrails check leaves out the detail of its last findings in ID order, as `SightingBudget.checkRecord.fit` does. A trimmed finding keeps its ID, rule, severity, resolution, place and What to do, so what blocks is unchanged. Its Why here names how many files lost their detail and says that `git diff` shows them. A finding that trimming would not make smaller keeps its detail.
- A record that still passes the limit with every finding trimmed fails the guardrails check, with `RecordError` `recordTooLarge` and a fixed sentence that holds no finding's text. The review reads not reviewed, and its records export.
- Every check's record gets the same budget, not the guardrails alone. A static tool may write 16 MiB of output, so enough Biome, tsc or [cut at 2 KiB]

message.text: The budget exists to keep a check record within the store's `recordLimit`, so that the store never refuses the round's records after a verdict is stored. `fit` measures `finding.toJSON()` of the local findings, line 51, and `runCheck` applies it before adjudication, checks.ts:327. The bytes the store measures are those of the exported record. `ReviewRecords.check` rewrites each static sighting through `sighting()`, review-records.ts:431-439. That swaps Biome's and tsc's local message, What, Why here and What to do for `withheld` sentences, which are longer. Local: `withheldToolText`, about 105 characters, plus a Why here of about 75 and a What to do of about 50. Shared: `<check> reports <rule> here. <withheld>.` plus two copies of the 85-character `withheld`. So the measured quantity is smaller than the one being bounded, and a record the budget passed still grows past the limit.

explanation: {
					what: each.result.message.text,
					whyHere:
						each.result.advice?.whyHere ??
						(cause === "introduced"
							? `${tool} reports this at head but not at the base, so this change introduced it.`
							: `${tool} reports this at the base too, so it predates this change.`),

- **The relay batch.** Each check's record fits the store alone, but the relay carries a round's records in one batch of at most 8 MiB. Three valid 3 MiB check records pass the store and the verdict, and the relay then refuses the batch. The reader sees a refused relay, and the round's records are lost.
- **A projection smaller than the local findings.** The shared record replaces a static tool's text with fixed sentences. A check whose own text is long can fail as too large when its projected record would fit. The reader sees a failed check, and the review reads not reviewed.
- **A projection larger than the local findings.** For Biome and tsc, the projected fixed sentences are longer than the local text: 518 bytes against 487 for one finding's message and explanation. A static check whose local findings come within about 6% of the limit can pass the budget while its exported record is past it. The store then refuses the record after the verdict is stored. The reader sees a store error with exit code 2, and no verdict in CI.

explanation.what: The budget exists to keep a check record within the store's `recordLimit`, so that the store never refuses the round's records after a verdict is stored. `fit` measures `finding.toJSON()` of the local findings, line 51, and `runCheck` applies it before adjudication, checks.ts:327. The bytes the store measures are those of the exported record. `ReviewRecords.check` rewrites each static sighting through `sighting()`, review-records.ts:431-439. That swaps Biome's and tsc's local message, What, Why here and What to do for `withheld` sentences, which are longer. Local: `withheldToolText`, about 105 characters, plus a Why here of about 75 and a What to do of about 50. Shared: `<check> reports <rule> here. <withheld>.` plus two copies of the 85-character `withheld`. So the measured quantity is smaller than the one being bounded, and a record the budget passed still grows past the limit.
explanation.whatToDo: Measure what the store measures. Have `runCheck`, or the budget, size each finding as `ReviewRecords` will project it (the `sighting()`/`shareable()` projection plus the `status` field `producerSightings` adds), or the whole check record built from the result. Alternatively, size the store-side check once the record is built and fail the check with `recordTooLarge` before adjudication stores a verdict.
explanation.whyHere: This change adds the budget to every check as its fix for issue #605. The head decision's own ruling says a record that cannot fit fails its check closed, and the review reads not reviewed. For Biome and tsc the budget passes local findings whose export is too large. So the failure #605 set out to end, a store error with a verdict of findings already stored, still happens, now behind a guard that claims to prevent it. The decision lists this as a known limit and defers it to issue #626. That defers the defect; it does not answer it.

properties.failureScenario: A head adds or changes enough code that Biome reports about 8,000 introduced findings under long paths, so the local findings' canonical JSON is about 3.9 MiB, within 6% of `SightingBudget.checkRecord.bytes`. `runCheck` calls `fit`. Line 60 sees the local total under the budget and returns the findings unchanged. Adjudication stores a verdict of blocking findings. At export, `ReviewRecords.check` projects each sighting with the longer withheld sentences, so the check record's canonical bytes pass 4 MiB. `SharedRecord.storable()` (record.ts:328) throws `invalidRecord` in the store's `add`. The review exits with a store error (exit code 2, by the decision's own account). The round's records never reach the shared store, and CI shows no verdict. This is the outcome the maintainer's ruling said must instead fail the check closed.
